I've been farming this land in Quzhou for 25 years, and I know what works here on the North China Plain. My 20 mu isn't huge, but it's enough to feed my family and bring in some cash if I manage it right. With five mouths to feed and some family members working off-farm, I can't afford to take big risks or spend all my time in the fields. I need a system that's reliable and doesn't break my back.

Here's how I see it: wheat and maize are my bread and butter. The wheat-maize double cropping has been the backbone of my farm for decades. That rotation goes on my best land — about 14 mu. Wheat in the winter and spring, then maize right after the June harvest. I always use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize. The yield difference is real, and after 25 years I don't need any convincing. For the remaining 6 mu, I'll grow stevia. The buyers come through every year, and the income per mu can be decent if the leaves are good quality. It also doesn't need to fit into the tight wheat-maize window.

For the wheat, I'll do rotary tillage before sowing in October and put down base fertilizer. I'll irrigate four times: once before winter to protect the seedlings from the cold, then at jointing, heading, and grain filling. That's what this well is for. I won't skip the jointing water — that's when the yield is made. For fertilizer, I'll use about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus phosphorus and potassium. I learned a long time ago that you can't just pile on nitrogen; the wheat lodges and you lose more than you gain.

For the summer maize, timing is everything. After the wheat comes off in early June, I need to get the maize in the ground fast before the rains stop. I'll use a no-till seeder to plant directly into the wheat stubble. It saves me three or four days, keeps the soil moisture, and I've noticed the stubble helps keep the soil cooler. Two irrigations will do — one if it gets dry at the jointing stage, and one at flowering if the summer drought hits. The maize will get about 16 kg nitrogen per mu. Hybrid seed is non-negotiable; the yield is just too much higher.

For the stevia on the 6 mu, I'll prepare that land with rotary tillage in early spring and plant in April. Stevia needs water but hates waterlogging, so I'll irrigate carefully — maybe three times through the growing season. It also needs potassium for leaf quality, so I'll give it a bit more K than the cereals. I'll harvest the leaves twice, once in summer and once in autumn before the frost.

I don't spray pesticides more than I have to — two or three times for wheat, twice for maize, twice for stevia. The pests come every year, but over-spraying wastes money and I don't like the smell anyway.
